title: One, two, three
hook: the Tao produced one, one two, two three, three all things; all carry yin and embrace yang (Tao Te Ching 42)

segments.voice: Yesterday, if they didn't laugh: chapter forty-one says that if some people didn't laugh at the way, it wouldn't be the way. Your line was they laugh. Did anyone smile at your odd little practice, and did you keep it? Day one thousand one hundred four.

One, two, three. It's how a child counts before jumping into a pool, how a band counts in a song, how a race begins. Chapter forty-two of the Tao Te Ching counts too, and in a handful of words it gets from the way to everything there is. Then, right after the counting, it names two words that have traveled far beyond the book, onto t-shirts and tattoos and necklaces split in half: yin and yang. Today we read them where this chapter puts them.
screen: `ONE, TWO, THREE.` → `FROM THE WAY TO EVERYTHING.` → `YIN AND YANG, IN THEIR SETTING.`

segments.voice: First, the count. In James Legge's translation: "The Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three; Three produced All things." It reads like a family tree, or a seed becoming a forest. Second, the honest part. The chapter never says what one, two and three are. Readers have filled the gap in different ways. Some take one as the first unity, two as yin and yang, and three as what happens when the two blend. Others leave the numbers as a rhythm: from one, many. The text itself stays quiet, and it's fine to let it. Third, the two words. The chapter says all things carry yin on their backs and hold yang in their arms, and a blending breath brings them into harmony. Legge doesn't even write yin and yang; he renders them as the Obscurity and the Brightness. Either way, the picture isn't a fight between good and bad. Every single thing carries both, at once, and the harmony comes from the blend, not from one side winning. Fourth, in a single day. It's easy to sort a day into opposites and want only one side: rest and not work, praise and not criticism, sunshine and not shade. The chapter's picture is gentler. You carry both. Effort and ease in the same breath. Strength and tenderness in the same person. A sad morning and a good afternoon in the same day. The work isn't to get rid of one. It's to let the two find their balance.
screen: `THE TAO PRODUCED ONE.` · `THE TEXT DOESN'T SAY WHAT THEY ARE.` · `ALL THINGS CARRY YIN, EMBRACE YANG.` · `BOTH SIDES IN ONE DAY.` · then, large: `CARRY BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a balance of opposites. Settle where you are and start with the breath. In, then out. Neither one is the good one; you need both. Now look around the room. Find light and shadow side by side. Then check your body: somewhere is tense, somewhere is soft. Don't fix either. Just notice that both are there at once, and let the breath move between them. The bell holds the time.
Yin yang. In chapter forty-two, the two that every single thing carries at once, brought into harmony by a blending breath. Today's word.
Your line: carry both. When today hands you two opposites at once, a hard task and a kind word, a tired body and a clear head, try holding both instead of choosing. Day one thousand one hundred four.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter forty-two's yin and yang as a picture of opposites held together in balance, and some use it as a reminder not to cling to one side of a pair.

fork.setup: a day hands you a hard task and good news at the same time. what does chapter forty-two's picture suggest?
options: focus only on the good news.
carry both, and let them balance.
push the hard task away until tomorrow.
fork.reveal: the chapter says all things carry yin and embrace yang together. the harmony comes from the blend, not from one side winning.
